name: Francisco Penzotti
place: Uruguay, Peru, and other Latin American countries
title: Francisco Penzotti: carrying the Bible along the roads of Latin America
description: An Italian immigrant in Uruguay, the work of distributing Bibles, and a community that persevered in Callao.

sections.heading: From Montevideo to the roads of the continent
paragraphs: Francisco Penzotti emigrated from Italy to Uruguay. In Montevideo he met Methodist missionaries and, after his conversion, began serving among Protestant communities. His journey reminds us that the history of Latin American Christianity also includes migrations, encounters, and people who learned to live out their faith in a new land.

During the 1880s he traveled through several South American countries as a preacher and Bible distributor. He worked with colporteurs, traveling sellers of Bible literature, among them Andrew Milne. His journeys combined contact with readers and the forming of communities with the hardships of getting around the continent.

sections.heading: A community during imprisonment
paragraphs: In 1888 he began gathering a congregation in Callao, Peru. The work met opposition, and Penzotti was imprisoned. The case of 1890–1891 drew international attention; the community kept meeting while its pastor was in prison. He was released after about eight months in prison.

His later work included Central America. He died in Buenos Aires in 1925. Methodist memory remembers him for distributing the Bible and for his pastoral service; to understand the conflicts he went through, it is wise also to study the legal and religious conditions in each country, without turning an entire population into an adversary.

reflection: Second Timothy 2:9–10 shows Paul in prison and declares that “the word of God cannot be chained.” This does not automatically equate every experience of imprisonment with the apostle’s, but it reminds us that Christian witness does not depend on the freedom or strength of a single person.

The story of Callao invites us to value the congregation together with its pastor. Visiting, standing with others, and keeping Bible reading going are shared forms of service. Defending freedom of conscience requires offering other people the respect we want for our own community.
review_note: The documented course of his life is summarized without inventing dialogue or conversions. The sources come from Methodist memory; opposition is not generalized to all Catholics or to all of Peruvian society.
